title: Your charity

segments.voice: Yesterday, the halaqah. Your line: learn together. Did you share one thing you learned, and hear what someone else made of it? A circle meets again and again. Today, a gift that does the same. Day one thousand four hundred six.

On a kitchen shelf, between the rice and the tea, sits an old jam jar with a strip of tape on it. Someone has written one word on the tape in marker: sadaqah. Every evening, whoever empties their pockets drops in the loose change. Nobody makes a speech about it. Once a month the jar is emptied and the money goes somewhere: a food bank, a neighbor's medical bill, a well. The jar is not impressive. It is just always there, filling slowly. Today, setting a regular sadaqah.
screen: `A JAR BETWEEN THE RICE AND THE TEA.` → `LOOSE CHANGE, EVERY EVENING.` → `NOT IMPRESSIVE. ALWAYS THERE.`

segments.voice: Start by telling two gifts apart. Zakat is the required one: a set share of wealth, owed by those who have enough, to the groups the Qur'an names. Sadaqah is the open one. It is voluntary, it has no minimum, and it can be given at any hour. Next, the rhythm. Surah al-Baqarah praises those who spend their wealth by night and by day, in secret and in the open, and says their reward is with their Lord. By night and by day: not one event, but a pattern running through the hours. That is the case for the jar. A small gift that keeps going shapes the giver in a way a single grand gesture may not. Third, the size of it. Earlier in the same surah, the Qur'an compares money spent in Allah's way to a single grain that grows seven ears, with a hundred grains in each ear. The picture is of something small put in the ground and multiplied. The same surah says that giving openly is good, and giving quietly to the poor is better for you. So a regular, quiet gift has two things going for it at once. Last, what counts. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says every good deed is a charity. Another hadith in Bukhari names some: a good word, helping someone onto their mount, removing something harmful from the road. Sadaqah is wider than money. So a regular sadaqah can be a monthly transfer, a weekly visit, or a jar of coins. What matters is that it comes back around.
screen: `ZAKAT REQUIRED, SADAQAH OPEN.` · `BY NIGHT AND BY DAY.` · `ONE GRAIN, SEVEN EARS.` · `EVERY GOOD DEED IS A CHARITY.`

segments.voice: The practice: set up a small regular gift. First, a quiet minute. Breathe in, and out, and let your hands open on your knees, palms up. Notice how little effort it takes to hold them open. Now think about what you could give regularly without strain: a small amount each week or month, an hour of time, a meal for someone. Keep it small enough that you'd never be tempted to skip it. Then ask where it would go. A cause near you, a person you know, a place you trust. Let one answer settle. If you pray, you can ask Allah to accept it. After the bell, set it up: a recurring transfer, a reminder on your phone, or a jar with a strip of tape. The bell holds the time.
Your charity. A regular sadaqah, small enough to keep, given again and again, quietly. Today's word.
Your line: regular giving. Today, do one small good deed that costs no money at all, and count it. Tomorrow, your character. Day one thousand four hundred six.

howItsDone: Alongside the required zakat, Muslims give sadaqah, voluntary charity, in any amount and at any time; some set up a regular gift, weekly or monthly, following surah al-Baqarah's praise of those who give by night and by day.

fork.setup: you have a little to give. you could give it all at once, once a year, or a small amount every week. which fits al-Baqarah's picture of the giver?
options: the gift that runs through the weeks.
fork.reveal: al-Baqarah praises those who spend by night and by day, in secret and in the open (2:274): giving as a pattern, not one event. a jar of coins qualifies.

original.note: Arabic: voluntary charity, given at any time.

trapdoor: what you thought: charity is a big donation, once in a while.
what it means: sadaqah, voluntary and open, best kept small and regular, and wider than money.
what a scholar hears: al-Baqarah's givers by night and by day, its grain of seven ears, giving quietly as better for the giver, and every good deed as a charity.
